passages.happening:
“Indeed, my eyes have seen all this; my ears have heard and understood. What you know, I also know; I am not inferior to you. Yet I desire to speak to the Almighty and argue my case before God” (verses 1-3).

“You, however, smear with lies; you are all worthless physicians. If only you would remain silent; for that would be your wisdom!” (verses 4-5).

Then Job turns their defense of God against them. “Will you speak wickedly on God’s behalf or speak deceitfully for Him?” (verse 7). Would they show God partiality? Could they deceive him as they might deceive a man? “Surely He would rebuke you if you secretly showed partiality” (verse 10). “Your maxims are proverbs of ashes; your defenses are defenses of clay” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Ancient medicine combined practical remedies, ointments and plasters, with prayers and ritual. The word for smear suggests plastering over, as if the friends were covering the wound with lies instead of treating it.

Witnesses in a court were expected to tell the truth, and a false witness could face the penalty he had sought for the accused. Job applies that to his friends. They are acting as God's advocates, and in doing it they are bending the truth to defend him. Job warns that God does not want such a defense and will expose it. It is a remarkable claim. In the ancient world, defending the gods was normally thought to please them.

The point holds for every age. False comfort offered in God's name is a sin against God. Speaking of God must be truthful, even when the truth is uncomfortable.

Proverbs of ashes are sayings that crumble, and defenses of clay are like a wall of mud brick: they look solid and do not hold.
passages.later: The law dealt hard with a lying witness: ‘if the witness is proven to be a liar who has falsely accused his brother, you must do to him as he intended to do to his brother’ (Deuteronomy 19:18-19). In the end God will say the friends have not spoken rightly about him (Job 42:7).
passages.asks: Job told his friends that silence would have been their wisdom. Ask whether you have ever defended God by saying something that was not true. And ask what it would mean to tell the truth about God even when it leaves questions open.

passages.t: Hope, or defiance, before God's face
passages.happening:
“Be silent, and I will speak. Then let come to me what may. Why do I put myself at risk and take my life in my own hands?” (verses 13-14).

“Though He slay me, I will hope in Him. I will still defend my ways to His face. Moreover, this will be my salvation, for no godless man can appear before Him” (verses 15-16).

“Listen carefully to my words; let my declaration ring in your ears. Behold, now that I have prepared my case, I know that I will be vindicated” (verses 17-18).
passages.hearers:
This is a turning point. In chapter 9, a lawsuit with God seemed hopeless. Now it is a decision. Job is no longer only lamenting. He is pressing for a hearing, and the same resolve will grow through chapter 23 and end in the oath of chapter 31. When God finally speaks in chapter 38, he answers the man who asked for this hearing.

Taking one's life in one's hands was an idiom for exposing oneself to mortal danger. Ancient people held that no one could see God and live (Exodus 33:20), and Job knows that going before God's face is dangerous.

To prepare a case, in verse 18, is a legal phrase, to set out one's arguments in order, as soldiers are drawn up in ranks.

Verse 16 is remarkable. Job believes that being able to come before God at all will be his rescue, since the godless cannot. His hope is not in escaping God but in appearing before him. Salvation, yeshuah, comes from the same root as the name Joshua.
passages.later: Paul's words in prison repeat the wording of Job 13:16 in the Greek Old Testament: ‘my distress will turn out for my deliverance’ (Philippians 1:19). Like Job, he expected to be cleared before God whatever human judges decided.
passages.hard:
Does verse 15 speak of hope, or of no hope?

The famous line rests on a small difference in the Hebrew. The consonants written in the traditional text, called the ketiv, what is written, spell lo meaning not. That gives a sense like this: God will slay Job, and Job has no hope, yet he will defend his ways to God's face. Jewish scribes also kept a reading to be spoken aloud, the qere, what is read, which spells lo differently, meaning in him. That gives the familiar reading, that Job will hope in God. Both words sound the same in Hebrew.

Some ancient versions, such as the Latin Vulgate, and most English translations follow the spoken reading. Many modern scholars and some translations prefer the written one. On either reading, Job is going before God to argue his case with no guarantee of survival. The difference is whether that act is described as hope or as defiance. The rest of the chapter, in which Job expects to be vindicated (verse 18), is often cited in support of hope. These notes take no side.
passages.asks: Job resolved to go to God's face, whatever it cost him. Ask whether you have held on to God while God seemed to be the source of your pain. And ask what it would mean for you to keep coming before him rather than staying away.

passages.t: Why do You hide Your face?
passages.happening:
Now Job speaks to God. “Only grant these two things to me, so that I need not hide from You: Withdraw Your hand from me, and do not let Your terror frighten me. Then call me, and I will answer, or let me speak, and You can reply” (verses 20-22).

“How many are my iniquities and sins? Reveal to me my transgression and sin. Why do You hide Your face and consider me as Your enemy?” (verses 23-24). Would God chase a windblown leaf, or dry chaff? He writes bitter charges against Job and makes him inherit the sins of his youth. He puts his feet in the stocks and watches every path.

“So man wastes away like something rotten, like a moth-eaten garment” (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
Job asks for two things: that God would take his hand away and stop terrifying him. Then, he says, the hearing could begin, with either side speaking first.

His question in verse 23 is honest. He does not claim to be sinless. He asks to be shown what he has done, if anything, that could explain this.

Stocks for the feet were wooden restraints used to hold prisoners. The meaning of the last line of verse 27 is uncertain; it may refer to marking or tracking prisoners.

The chapter ends with a quiet image of decay, a moth-eaten garment, which leads straight into the meditation on human frailty in chapter 14.
passages.later: The psalms pray the same question: “Why, O LORD, do You stand far off? Why do You hide in times of trouble?” (Psalm 10:1).
passages.asks: Job asked God to show him his sin, if there was any. Ask whether you are willing to pray that prayer honestly. And ask how you might bring your anger to God himself, rather than turning it on the people around you.
